text: English ships reach a coast that is already somebody's home, and that arrival gets two and a half hours rather than a scene. Terrence Malick treats the seventeenth century as a problem of attention: what the settlers look at, what they cannot read, how long grass and river water can hold a frame before they stop being scenery and become the subject. The Academy Award here went to the cinematography, which is the correct prize, since the picture carries most of the reasoning. John Smith is present and the settlement is present, but the encounter plays less as collision than as a long misreading conducted in fine weather, by people on both sides who believe they are behaving well. Patience is the cost of admission. What it buys is a version of contact that nobody has tidied into a story.

A young musician with more ambition than material climbs into a van with a band whose leader he cannot read. Lenny Abrahamson balances Frank on an awkward hinge: the comedy of amateurs playing at genius, and the harder thing beneath it, which is that some people make music because it is the only arrangement of the world they can live inside. Frank himself is not a puzzle with a solution but a man who declines to be explained, and the film holds that line to the end. Ninety-five minutes, no fat on it. An audience prize at IFFR is a funny destiny for a story about the gap between a band and the crowd it half wants, and the funniness is the point: the joke and the ache keep turning up in the same sentence.

An actress who no longer gets offers takes one more job, and the film she is in changes medium partway through. Ari Folman begins with a plain transaction, a woman told what she is worth now and handed the conditions that come with the figure, then follows those conditions out of the industry drama into science fiction and finally into the animation that the European Film Award recognised. Two hours, and the subject throughout is consent: what a person owes an agreement she signed without reading the far end of it. The dryness keeps it upright. Nobody consoles her, the terms are never reopened, and the drawn world that widens out around her proves no kinder than the photographed one, only easier to keep looking at.

Frida is six, and the year in the title belongs to her rather than to history. Carla Simón puts a child who has just lost her mother into a farmhouse full of people who are kind, busy and not hers, then stays inside the child's range of understanding, where questions go unanswered because the adults are in the next room and mid-sentence. Estiu 1993 is in Catalan, and the Gaudí Award names that language in the prize itself, which suits a film so alert to how a household talks when it has forgotten who is listening. One summer, almost no plot in the usual sense: a girl working out what is hers now and what she is permitted to want. The tenderness and the cruelty share a source, which is that everyone here is improvising.

A family cannot sit down to eat until the priest arrives, and the priest is not there yet. Cristi Puiu gives that wait 173 minutes: a memorial lunch a year after the father's death, a flat with more relatives than chairs, a neurologist just back from Paris, a wife collected on the way, a meal that keeps not beginning. Talk slides from who behaved how, to wars and world events, to whether the jacket fits, and back again, with nobody marking the change of subject. Doors keep opening on arguments that were already running in the next room. The length is not indulgence but a measurement, of how long a family needs before anyone says the thing they came to say, and of how much gets settled instead in a corridor.

Budapest, 1913, and a young woman presents herself for work at a hat shop that used to belong to her parents. László Nemes keeps Napszállta tight to what she can find out, which is little and never in sequence: a brother she had not known existed, a city that answers questions with further questions, a trade where everything is made to order and nothing is explained. The date does its own work. A year short of the catastrophe, the film lets the pressure sit in the corners instead of announcing it, and puts its two hours and seventeen minutes at street level, in crowds, behind one person who is always slightly behind the information. The millinery is exact, and the exactness is part of the trouble.

Christine travels to a shrine famous for cures, and the thing she is short of first is company. Jessica Hausner films the pilgrimage as an institution rather than a mystery: staff, volunteers, a timetable, rules of conduct, a group of people waiting in different measure for the same thing. Illness limits Christine to very small movements, so the performance lives in the face and in timing, and the European Film Award for acting matches what is actually on screen. The film takes belief seriously without taking a side. What it watches is the arithmetic that starts up among the hopeful once it is clear not everyone will be granted the same, and how quickly ordinary envy finds a footing in a holy place. It stays level all the way through.

A man goes into the water after someone who is drowning and comes back without him. Karim Aïnouz opens Praia do Futuro on that failure and then refuses to make a lesson of it: Donato meets a friend of the man he could not reach, and the acquaintance becomes a reason to leave, the work and the coast and everyone who knows him set down and walked away from. The film is patient with the walking away. What it will not grant is a clean exit, since the people with a claim on Donato have no intention of releasing it and arrive on their own schedule. In Portuguese, and far more interested in bodies, water and weather than in reasons for them. Rescue turns out to be the wrong word for almost anything anyone does here.

The ransom asked is more than everything the family owns, added together. Nalchik, 1998: the youngest son and his bride do not come home, a note arrives in the morning, and a small business built over years turns into a sum that has to be found. Kantemir Balagov keeps the emergency inside the community where the asking must be done, a Jewish family obliged to lay its private disaster in front of people who will help and who will remember having helped. Debt does the work that a villain would do in another kind of film. Two hours of negotiation at close quarters, among people who already know one another's business, and the film is as interested in what the asking costs as in whether the money is raised.

The garage might close any week now, and minding it is still a job. Josie does the minding, in a town where the same few cars pass at the same few hours, and Lenny Abrahamson gives that routine eighty-five minutes of close, unhurried attention. Then David arrives to work alongside him, the son of the boss's girlfriend, a teenager with friends and evenings to fill, and Josie, a grown man, finds that being included lifts him more than it safely should. The comedy is real and so is the wince, and Abrahamson refuses to hand over one without the other. What the film knows and Josie does not is how a small place reads an adult who spends his nights with teenagers and brings the beer, and it is in no hurry to say so.

A boarding school adds conscious eating to the timetable and hires a specialist to teach it. Miss Novak arrives with the calm of someone who has read the literature, five students take to her, and Jessica Hausner handles the whole arrangement with the composure of a school brochure. The comedy is in how reasonable everybody sounds. The thriller is in the fact that an institution has handed a question about children's bodies to a stranger with a syllabus while the parents paying for all of it are on another continent. The temperature of the thing never rises, which is what makes it frightening. The subject is authority: who is licensed to tell a young person what to want, and how little friction a good manner meets on the way.

Reza raises fish in fresh water, well away from town, on land that a company has decided it wants. He had already withdrawn from things; the ponds were the retirement, and ponds need water, which is the detail that pressure will find. Mohammad Rasoulof keeps the opposition corporate and diffuse, not a man to be faced down but an arrangement of obligations and favours closing from several directions while everyone stays courteous. The scenes are outdoors and quiet, in Persian, and the threat never has to raise its voice. The interest is not in whether Reza is right but in the running cost of staying right, paid in part by a wife and a son who never agreed to the principle and cannot get out from under it.

A divorced Romanian man acquires a hunting rifle, and the film built around that purchase runs three hours. Cristi Puiu spends them on everything a thriller removes: errands across town, stairs, waiting, parked cars, tasks that breed further tasks, conversations held in doorways because there is no reason to be let inside. The Romanian New Wave's patience with plain duration is pushed here to a place that is hard to sit in, since the ordinariness is not a contrast with the violence but its housing. Nothing is explained. The withholding is not a tease so much as the whole argument: motive is what courts and audiences require, and a man can be entirely legible from outside and shut all the way through.

A man decides that dying together would settle the question of love, and sets about finding someone who will agree. That Amour fou is filed as a comedy as well as a romance is not a clerical error. Jessica Hausner stages the courtship as a negotiation between people with excellent manners: Heinrich makes his case, Henriette listens, and the proposal is weighed about as a household matter is weighed, with attention to whose convenience it serves. Then she learns she is ill, and her interest sharpens for reasons that have very little to do with him. The evenness of tone is not coolness but accuracy, and it is what makes the comedy land. Ninety-six minutes, in German, and the laughter it earns arrives half a second late.
